newsitem.title: UK: Big players kick start London gas futures, but trade modest.
newsitem.headline: Big players kick start London gas futures, but trade modest.

text.p: The biggest players in the market helped kick-start the launch of Britain's first natural gas futures contract on Friday, but aside from a few flurries, overall trade was thin.

The International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) contract was busy at the 1000 GMT start, and saw another spate of trades just before the market's close at 1600 GMT. But in between the action was more subdued.
But the IPE said it was satisfied with business on the infant contract's first session, with deals done on all months of the contract.
"I'm pleasantly encouraged with the activity we've seen. It's nice to see all months have traded all the way out," said Richard Ward, the IPE's business development director.
A futures broker saw two positive factors after the first day -- a good range of players involved, and a depth in both bids and offers across the whole market, and not just the front months.

"There's been a bit of activity, with several different players involved," the broker said. "It could have been better but it's not that bad. Prices are down as fundamentals have driven the market. There's been a good two-way market, though there were more offers than bids."
Some of the UK's leading gas traders were in at the start.
"We had several trades executed immediately at the 1000 am opening of the market," said Louise Kitchen, director of gas trading at U.S. gas giant Enron Capital and Trade Resources .
Kitchen said Enron believed it had executed the first trade and had opened positions across all months to February 1998.
"Our reaction to the first morning is that we're quite pleased it all worked and we were able to transact successfully", she said.
As expected, the market opened closely in line with the UK spot market. The first trade in March was done at 14.900 pence a therm, with the market then tracking lower to close at 14.000 pence.
April, May, August and all months from October onwards also closed at the day's lows.
But dealers said that the market was more interested in the way the contract was working than with the price.
A total of 465 lots, representing 465,000 therms a day, were traded, spread reasonably evenly across all periods.

"We're pleasantly surprised by how it's all gone in terms of systems," said a trader with Britain's biggest gas trader Accord Energy, part of British Gas plc. "There have been no hiccups with quote vendors and no technical problems."
Accord had traded "small bits and pieces" on both side of the market with a view to stimulating trade, he said. "Basically we're optimistic for the future."
The contract trades in two session, from 10-12 gmt, and from 14-16 gmt.
